voices.title: Agent skill authoring — the base voice, read from two ingested papers
voices.description: The voice for writing and reviewing agent skills: what a SKILL.md's description must carry to be routed to at all, how much may sit in the body, where references and examples go, and what to do before trusting somebody else's skill. Twelve rules, every one cited to a page of an ingested paper. This is the SHARED BASE — the part the vendors agree on. Anything specific to one vendor's platform belongs in an override under `vendors/`, declaring this voice in its `extends` field.

sources.title: Authoring Agent Skills: A Software-Engineering Approach
What Keeps Agent Skills from Being Reusable? Evidence from 138K SKILL.md Files

rules.title: The description states BOTH what the skill does and when to use it
rules.description: A description that names only the function cannot be routed to. State the operations and the triggering situations, in the concrete terms a real request would contain — "Drafts release notes from the pull requests merged between two version tags. Use when cutting a release…" rather than "Handles releases". This is the most prevalent defect in the public corpus and the only one whose harm has been measured end to end: R1.3 (missing trigger guidance) affects 52.3% of 138,133 skills, and R1-clean skills reach 88.5% hit@1 against 82.6% for R1-defective ones. A skill that is never selected has no other quality.
rules.quote: State both what the skill does and when it should be used, and include the concrete terms a relevant task would contain.

rules.title: Write the description in the third person
rules.description: The description is read by the model as part of its own context, so first or second person degrades matching. "Reviews a diff for…", never "I review…" or "You can use this to…". This is a routing property, not a style preference — the same sentence in the wrong person is a worse trigger.
rules.quote: Write it in the third person, since it is read by the model as part of its own context, and a first or second person voice can degrade matching.

rules.title: Keep the body under about 500 lines
rules.description: The body enters the context window whole, the moment the skill is selected. Past roughly five hundred lines it starts displacing the conversation and the other context the task needs, so length is a cost paid at every invocation rather than a one-off. Longer material belongs in a reference file, which costs nothing until it is read.
rules.quote: The body should stay under about five hundred lines, a few thousand tokens, so that once loaded it does not crowd out the conversation and other context

rules.title: Add only what the model does not already know
rules.description: Explaining what the model already understands is not harmless padding: every sentence competes for context once the body is loaded, so a paragraph restating general knowledge displaces one carrying a project convention. Write the non-obvious procedure, the specific file location, the rule that must hold — and delete the rest.
rules.quote: Assume the model already holds general knowledge, and add only what it does not have: project conventions, non-obvious procedures, specific file locations, rules that must hold.

rules.title: Reference files are linked ONE level deep, never chained
rules.description: Link every reference file directly from the body. A file that links onward to another may be reached by a partial read, and the model then acts on incomplete information — a failure that looks like the skill working, because something was read. The depth limit is what makes a partial read safe.
rules.quote: those files should not chain onward to further files, because the model may preview a deeply linked file with a partial read and then act on incomplete information

rules.title: A reference file over ~100 lines opens with a table of contents
rules.description: A partial read of a long reference shows its opening. If that opening is a table of contents, the reader learns the file's full scope even when it never reaches the end; without one it learns only the first section and cannot tell what it missed.
rules.quote: For any reference file longer than about one hundred lines, place a short table of contents at the top so the model can see the full scope even on a partial read

rules.title: Give ONE default and name the exception
rules.description: A body that lists alternatives without ranking them leaves the model choosing on no grounds, which makes its behaviour vary run to run for reasons the author cannot see. State the default, then state the specific condition under which something else applies.
rules.quote: Offering many alternatives leaves the model to choose without grounds, so give one default and name the exception.

rules.title: State every dependency the skill assumes
rules.description: A skill that assumes a package, a binary or a path is present fails on the machine where it is not — and fails at the point of use, having already been selected. Name what must be installed, and prefer a check that reports the gap over a step that dies on it.
rules.quote: Assuming a package is installed fails when it is not, so state dependencies explicitly.

rules.title: Write the evaluations before the skill
rules.description: Run the model on representative tasks WITHOUT the skill and record where it actually fails. Those failures are the test cases; the skill is the minimum instruction set that passes them. Written the other way round, a skill documents what its author imagined the model could not do, and the two sets overlap less than they appear to.
rules.quote: Write evaluations before writing the skill.

rules.title: Read a third-party skill in full before using it
rules.description: A skill carries instructions and may carry code, both of which the agent can act on. Installing one from outside the project without reading it is running unreviewed content in the agent's own voice, where it is indistinguishable from the project's own guidance.
rules.quote: a skill from a third party should be read in full before it is used.

rules.title: Do not repeat the skill's name as the body's first heading
rules.description: The name is already in the frontmatter and already in the model's context at level one. Repeating it as the opening heading spends body lines restating what the reader has, and it is the second most common defect in the public corpus at 44.3%. Open with what the reader does not yet have.
rules.quote: The three most prevalent individual defects are all spec violations: R1.3 miss- ing trigger guidance (52.3%), R2.4 name-as-heading dupli- cation (44.3%), and R3.2 too many inline examples (32.1%).

rules.title: Too many inline examples belong in a reference file
rules.description: Examples are the easiest thing to add and the most expensive to carry, because they sit in the body and load on every invocation. R3.2 affects 32.1% of public skills. Keep the one example that disambiguates the instruction; move the rest to a reference the body links, where they cost nothing until needed.
rules.quote: The three most prevalent individual defects are all spec violations: R1.3 miss- ing trigger guidance (52.3%), R2.4 name-as-heading dupli- cation (44.3%), and R3.2 too many inline examples (32.1%).

voices.title: Agent skill authoring — Claude override

MODEL-SPECIFIC by the owner's ruling (bean rkqp): a vendor's advice is evidence about that vendor's platform. Provenance ASSERTION: a publisher describing its own product. Rules the base already carries — much of it traceable to this very document (the ~500-line body, one-level references, a table of contents over ~100 lines, third-person descriptions, evaluations before instructions) — are inherited through extends, not repeated. Conformance is an agentic review, never a schema gate.

sources.title: Skill authoring best practices | Claude Platform Docs (captured 2026-09-20)

rules.title: name ≤ 64 characters of lowercase, digits and hyphens; description ≤ 1,024 characters; no XML tags in either
rules.description: Claude validates the SKILL.md front matter: name at most 64 characters, lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only, no XML tags and no reserved words; description non-empty, at most 1,024 characters, no XML tags. A skill that breaks these does not load on Claude, which is why this is a vendor rule — other platforms state different limits or none.
rules.quote: The SKILL.md frontmatter requires name and description fields with specific validation rules: name : Maximum 64 characters, lowercase letters/numbers/hyphens only, no XML tags, no reserved words description : Maximum 1,024 characters, non-empty, no XML tags

rules.title: Prefer a gerund name — processing-pdfs, not pdf-helper
rules.description: Anthropic's preferred form is the gerund (processing-pdfs, analyzing-spreadsheets); noun phrases (pdf-processing) and action-oriented names (process-pdfs) are acceptable alternatives. Pick one pattern for a whole collection: inconsistency within a collection is listed among the things to avoid.
rules.quote: Remember that the name field must use lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only. Good naming examples (gerund form): processing-pdfs analyzing-spreadsheets managing-databases testing-code writing-documentation Acceptable alternatives: Noun phrases: pdf-processing , spreadsheet-analysis Action-oriented: process-pdfs , analyze-spreadsheets

rules.title: No vague, generic or reserved names
rules.description: helper, utils and tools say nothing; documents, data and files are too generic to route on; names containing the reserved words (anthropic-helper, claude-tools) are refused.
rules.quote: Avoid: Vague names: helper , utils , tools Overly generic: documents , data , files Reserved words: anthropic-helper , claude-tools Inconsistent patterns within your skill collection

rules.title: Forward slashes in every file path, even on Windows
rules.description: scripts/helper.py, never scripts\helper.py: Unix-style paths work on every platform, Windows-style ones fail on Unix systems.
rules.quote: Always use forward slashes in file paths, even on Windows: ✓ Good: scripts/helper.py , reference/guide.md ✗ Avoid: scripts\helper.py , reference\guide.md Unix-style paths work across all platforms, while Windows-style paths cause errors on Unix systems.

rules.title: Every configuration value in a bundled script says why it is that value
rules.description: A magic number in a script is a value Claude cannot reason about: if the author does not know why it is right, the model cannot determine it either. Justify and document each constant (Ousterhout's 'voodoo constants').
rules.quote: Configuration parameters should also be justified and documented to avoid "voodoo constants" (Ousterhout's law). If you don't know the right value, how will Claude determine it?

rules.title: For a complex, open-ended change: plan in a structured form, validate the plan with a script, then execute
rules.description: The intermediate plan is the checkable artefact — mistakes (a non-existent field, a conflicting value, a missed requirement) are caught before anything is changed, not after.
rules.quote: When Claude performs complex, open-ended tasks, it can make mistakes. The "plan-validate- execute" pattern catches errors early by having Claude first create a plan in a structured format, then validate that plan with a script before executing it.

rules.title: One term per concept, throughout the skill
rules.description: Choose a term — 'API endpoint', 'field', 'extract' — and never alternate it with a synonym inside one skill; a variant reads to the model as a different thing.
rules.quote: Use consistent terminology Choose one term and use it throughout the Skill: Good - Consistent: Always "API endpoint" Always "field" Always "extract"

rules.title: Write the skill with one Claude instance and test it with another
rules.description: Anthropic's authoring loop: 'Claude A' helps design and refine the instructions; 'Claude B', a separate instance with the skill loaded, uses it on real tasks and exposes what is missing. Begin by doing the task once without a skill and noting the context you kept supplying — that is the skill's content.
rules.quote: Claude ("Claude A") to create a Skill that is used by other instances ("Claude B"). Claude A helps you design and refine instructions, while Claude B tests them in real tasks.

voices.title: Agent skill authoring — Gemini CLI override
voices.description: What Gemini CLI's own documentation adds to the shared base voice (agent-skill-authoring): its loading budget in words, its degrees-of-freedom rule, its folder names, script ergonomics and security. MODEL-SPECIFIC by the owner's ruling (bean rkqp, 2026-09-20): a vendor's advice is evidence about that vendor's platform, so it is a separate voice extending the base rather than caveats folded into it — a rule that turns out to be Gemini-only can then be dropped without touching the rest. Provenance is ASSERTION: a publisher describing its own product, revisable without notice. Rules the base already states (description carries function and trigger; read third-party skills before installing) are inherited through extends, not repeated. Conformance is an agentic review, never a schema gate — the owner's instruction, because 'best practice' drifts.

sources.title: Agent Skill best practices | Gemini CLI (captured 2026-09-20, page last updated 2026-04-30)

rules.title: A description is distinct from every other skill's — and from what the model does anyway
rules.description: Gemini CLI routes on the description alone, so two skills whose descriptions cover the same requests compete for them, and a description that restates a general capability of the model gives the router no reason to load the skill at all. Check a new description against the descriptions already installed, not only against the skill's own body.
rules.quote: Avoid overlap: Ensure your skill descriptions are distinct from one another and from the general capabilities of the model.

rules.title: Budget the three loading levels in WORDS: ~100 always loaded, under 5k on trigger
rules.description: Gemini CLI states its budget per level and in words: the name and description are always in context (~100 words), the SKILL.md body is loaded only when the skill triggers (under 5,000 words), and bundled resources only as needed. The base voice's '~500 lines' comes from a different source and a different unit; on Gemini CLI the word budget is the vendor's own figure. Neither is a hard limit the platform enforces — both are the publisher's guidance.
rules.quote: 1. Metadata (name + description): Always in context (~100 words). 2. SKILL.md body: Loaded only after the skill triggers (<5k words). 3. Bundled resources: Loaded only as needed by the model.

rules.title: Match how prescriptive a step is to how fragile it is
rules.description: Three levels: text instructions where several approaches are valid, pseudocode or a parameterised script where one pattern is preferred, and a specific script with few parameters where the operation is fragile or the sequence MUST be followed. Writing a fragile step as free prose is the failure this prevents; so is scripting a judgement call.
rules.quote: Degrees of freedom Match the level of instruction specificity to the task’s fragility. High freedom (text-based instructions): Use when multiple approaches are valid or decisions depend heavily on context. Medium freedom (pseudocode or scripts with parameters): Use when a preferred pattern exists but some variation is acceptable. Low freedom (specific scripts, few parameters): Use when operations are fragile and error-prone, or a specific sequence MUST be followed.

rules.title: A task a script can do is a script in scripts/, not prose
rules.description: If the step is deterministic — run a linter, fetch from an API — bundle it as a script under scripts/ and have the body call it, rather than describing the commands for the model to reproduce each time.
rules.quote: Use scripts for deterministic tasks: If a task can be automated with a script (for example, running a linter, fetching data from an API), bundle it in the scripts/ folder.

rules.title: A bundled script's output is written for a model to read
rules.description: Suppress verbose tracebacks and end with a clear, short success or failure message. The reader of a skill script's stdout is the agent, and a stack trace is context it pays for without learning what to do next.
rules.quote: Agentic ergonomics: Ensure scripts output LLM-friendly stdout. Suppress verbose tracebacks and provide clear, concise success/failure messages.

rules.title: Boilerplate the agent must reproduce exactly lives in assets/
rules.description: Common file headers and boilerplate go in assets/ as templates, so every run produces the same output rather than the model's recollection of it.
rules.quote: Provide templates: Include common file headers or boilerplate code in the assets/ folder to ensure the agent produces consistent output.

rules.title: SKILL.md is required; scripts/, references/ and assets/ are the optional sub-folders
rules.description: Gemini CLI's layout: SKILL.md (core instructions and metadata) is the only required file; executable logic goes in scripts/, documentation loaded on demand in references/, templates and other non-executable resources in assets/. Other vendors name these folders differently — Antigravity documents examples/ and resources/ — which is why this is a vendor rule and not a base one.
rules.quote: my-skill/ ├── SKILL.md (Required) Core instructions and metadata ├── scripts/ (Optional) Executable logic (Node.js, Python, etc.) ├── references/ (Optional) Documentation to be loaded as needed └── assets/ (Optional) Templates and non-executable resources

rules.title: Keep the body procedural; reference material, schemas and examples go in references/
rules.description: The body holds the core procedure. Detailed reference material, schemas and examples move to separate files in references/, loaded only when needed — the vendor's own folder name for what the base voice calls a reference file.
rules.quote: Best practice: Keep the SKILL.md body focused on core procedural instructions. Move detailed reference material, schemas, and examples into separate files in a references/ directory.

rules.title: No API key or password in a skill's scripts or documentation
rules.description: A skill is shared and installed by others; a credential written into it is published with it.
rules.quote: Avoid hardcoded secrets: Never include API keys or passwords in your skill’s scripts or documentation.

rules.title: Keep a skill as narrow as it can be
rules.description: The narrower the skill, the smaller the damage when it is wrong. A skill that does several things fails in several places at once.
rules.quote: Limit scope: Design skills to be as focused as possible to minimize the potential impact of errors.

voices.title: Agent skill authoring — OpenAI override
voices.description: What OpenAI's 'Skills in OpenAI API' cookbook notebook adds to the shared base voice agent-skill-authoring: front matter as the router, explicit use/don't-use routing with negative examples, scripts that behave like tiny CLIs, verification in SKILL.md, what may leave over the network, version pinning, and the platform's upload limits. MODEL-SPECIFIC by the owner's ruling (bean rkqp): a vendor's advice is evidence about that vendor's platform. Provenance ASSERTION: a publisher describing its own product. Read from the full notebook (ingested through the notebook rung, MIT-licensed), not the one-page PDF capture skills-in-openai-api, which is almost all code. Rules the base already carries — description states function and trigger, one default, state dependencies — are inherited through extends, not repeated. Conformance is an agentic review, never a schema gate.

sources.title: Skills in OpenAI API — OpenAI Cookbook notebook (fetched 2026-09-30, MIT)

rules.title: name and description live in the SKILL.md front matter, because that is what OpenAI routes on
rules.description: OpenAI reads each skill's name and description from its front matter and puts them in the prompt context, so a skill is found and chosen by those two fields alone. A description written only in the body is invisible to routing. The base voice says WHAT a description must state; this is where OpenAI requires it to be.
rules.quote: OpenAI models expect names and descriptions to come from frontmatter (important for discovery and routing).

rules.title: The body states when to use the skill AND when not to, with a few edge cases
rules.description: Explicit routing guidance in SKILL.md: a 'Use when…' list, a 'Don't use when…' list, and the edge cases between them. The negative half is the point: it is what stops a skill being invoked where it does not apply.
rules.quote: Add explicit routing guidance: “Use when…” vs. “Don’t use when…”, and a few key edge cases, all in `SKILL.md`.

rules.title: Give negative examples beside the positive ones
rules.description: Show cases where the skill should NOT be triggered, alongside the cases where it should. OpenAI states this improves routing accuracy.
rules.quote: Include negative examples (when the skill should *not* be triggered) alongside positive examples to improve routing accuracy.

rules.title: When routing misfires, revise the name, description and examples before the code
rules.description: An inconsistently invoked skill is a discovery problem first: iterate on the three things routing reads before changing what the skill does.
rules.quote: If routing feels inconsistent, iterate on name, description, and examples before changing code.

rules.title: A skill's script behaves like a small command-line tool
rules.description: It runs from the command line, prints deterministic stdout, fails loudly with a usage message or an error, and writes any outputs to known file paths. The model reads the output to decide what happened, so an ambiguous or silent script is a skill that cannot be verified.
rules.quote: Prints deterministic stdout

rules.title: Put concrete templates and worked examples inside the skill: inputs, commands, expected outputs
rules.description: The model reads these only when it invokes the skill, while the front matter stays in every prompt, so the detail belongs in the skill's files rather than in its description.
rules.quote: Add concrete templates and worked examples inside the skill (inputs → commands → expected outputs)

rules.title: SKILL.md states explicit verification steps and output checks
rules.description: Where execution is multi-step or brittle, the skill itself says how to check that each step worked, rather than trusting that it did.
rules.quote: add explicit verification steps and output checks in `SKILL.md`.

rules.title: Do not restate the skill's procedure in the system prompt
rules.description: A system prompt that repeats the whole procedure makes people bypass the skill and move logic into tool schemas, losing reuse, versioning and conditional invocation. The procedure lives in SKILL.md only.
rules.quote: If the system prompt repeats the entire procedure, people will:

rules.title: A skill that needs network access says what data may leave, beside a strict allowlist
rules.description: OpenAI calls skills plus open network access high-risk. When network access is unavoidable, the skill's instructions name what data is allowed to leave, and tool output is treated as untrusted.
rules.quote: If network access is required, pair allowlists with explicit “what data is allowed to leave” guidance.

rules.title: Pin the skill version, and the model with it, in production
rules.description: OpenAI keeps default_version and latest_version pointers. Production runs a named version, not whatever is latest, and pins the model beside it for reproducible behaviour.
rules.quote: Consider pinning the model and skill version together for reproducible behavior across deployments.

rules.title: One manifest, at most 500 files, a 50 MB zip, 25 MB per uncompressed file
rules.description: OpenAI's upload limits: exactly one SKILL.md (matched case-insensitively), at most 500 files per version, a zip of at most 50 MB, and no uncompressed file over 25 MB. A bundle outside them does not upload, which is why this is a vendor rule.
rules.quote: Exactly one manifest file allowed (`skill.md`/`SKILL.md`)

rules.title: A skill is for a procedure that has stabilised; one-offs and live data are not skills
rules.description: OpenAI's line: a one-off task belongs inline, live external data or side effects belong to a tool, and a procedure that changes daily is not ready to be a skill.
rules.quote: The procedure changes every day (skills shine when the workflow stabilizes).

voices.title: Linked data — how a coding agent emits and reviews JSON-LD
voices.description: The voice for a coding agent writing or reviewing code that EMITS JSON-LD: what makes the output linked data a processor can follow, rather than JSON that merely carries an @context. Six rules, each read from a held W3C text. Owner, 2026-10-01: "make sure that these issues are part of the one voice for jsonld" and "it is a voice for a coding agent, in a code authoring or review task". Every rule was found broken or fragile in this repository before it was written down (beans jcet, 9y9j): the PROV-O QA/QC reports carried prov:agent, prov:hadRole and prov:hadPlan as plain strings in all 100 activities, and the content context's @base resolves only because jsonld.js applies @base from a remote context.

sources.title: JSON-LD 1.1 — A JSON-based Serialization for Linked Data (W3C Recommendation, 16 July 2020)
PROV-O: The PROV Ontology (W3C Recommendation, 30 April 2013)
The PROV-JSONLD Serialization (W3C Member Submission, 25 August 2024; acknowledged, not endorsed)

rules.title: A property whose value is a node is emitted as a link, never as a string
rules.description: When the vocabulary defines a property as an OBJECT property (its value is another node: prov:agent, prov:hadRole, prov:hadPlan, prov:used), the emitted JSON-LD must make the value an IRI — through a term whose definition says "@type": "@id", or as {"@id": …}. A bare string under an uncoerced key expands to {"@value": …}, a literal: valid JSON-LD, but a graph in which the activity was done by the TEXT "owner" and nothing joins it to the actor. Review test: expand one emitted document with a real processor and look for @value where a node was meant.
rules.quote: Alternatively, the keyword @id or @vocab may be used as value to indicate that within the body of a JSON-LD document, a string value of a term coerced to @id or @vocab is to be interpreted as an IRI.

rules.title: Read the ontology for which properties take nodes; do not guess from the value's shape
rules.description: Whether a value is a node or a literal is decided by the vocabulary, not by what the string looks like. PROV-O marks each property op (object) or dp (data); prov:agent, prov:hadRole and prov:hadPlan are all op, so a role id like "user" is still a node reference. Code that decides by shape ("it has a slash, so it is an IRI") gets every short id wrong.
rules.quote: The superscripts op and dp denote that a property is an OWL object property or data property, respectively.

rules.title: A link names the node at its dereferenceable address; when it has none, say so instead of minting one
rules.description: Coercing a bare id to @id is not enough: "owner" then resolves against whatever @base is in force, naming a node that does not exist there. Emit the node's release address — <iriBase><version>/<path in its knowledge graph>[#fragment], the rule check:node-iris enforces — resolved through the OWNING instance's declaration. When the owner declares no iriBase, keep the value as a literal and record a finding naming the instance; an invented address is worse than an honest string.
rules.quote: IRIs are a fundamental concept of Linked Data, for nodes to be truly linked, dereferencing the identifier should result in a representation of that node.

rules.title: Do not rely on @base inside a context that documents reference by URL
rules.description: A context referenced by URL is an external context, and JSON-LD 1.1 ignores @base there. Measured 2026-10-01: jsonld.js applies it anyway, so this repository's relative @ids resolve today only through that processor's behaviour; a conforming processor resolves them against each document's own location. Emit absolute @ids, or put @base in the document's own (inline) context.
rules.quote: Please note that the @base will be ignored if used in external contexts.

rules.title: Hold every external context locally, pinned by hash; never fetch one while processing
rules.description: A context needed to understand a document is part of the document. Code that expands or verifies JSON-LD resolves context URLs through a documentLoader that serves a committed copy (with its sha256 recorded), and refuses anything else — the way publish:verify's localLoader does. A context that can only be had over the network makes the meaning of our data depend on somebody else's server being up and unchanged.
rules.quote: To protect against this, publishers should consider caching remote contexts for future use, or use the documentLoader to maintain a local version of such contexts.

rules.title: A compact-IRI key does not inherit another term's coercion
rules.description: Type coercion lives in a TERM's definition. Writing "prov:agent" as a key uses the prov prefix and no term definition, so it is NOT coerced even when the active context defines a term agent with "@type": "@id". Either use the defined term (agent) or define the compact IRI itself as a term. Mixing the two — PROV-JSONLD's context with prov:-prefixed keys — silently yields literals.
rules.quote: A compact IRI has the form of prefix:suffix and is used as a way of expressing an IRI without needing to define separate term definitions for each IRI contained within a common vocabulary identified by prefix.

rules.title: Emit PROV in PROV-JSONLD's shape, with its terms
rules.description: PROV is written with the PROV-JSONLD context and its terms: an Activity node with startTime/endTime, and each qualified relation as its own typed node — an Association carrying activity, agent, role and plan — so the context's coercions and @reverse mappings apply. The context is held locally (see ld-no-context-fetched-at-run-time). PROV-JSONLD is a W3C Member Submission, acknowledged and not endorsed by W3C; it is adopted here by owner decision (2026-10-01) because W3C publishes no JSON-LD context for PROV-O.
rules.quote: The JSON properties activity and plan map to the object properties prov:qualifiedAssociation and prov:hadPlan, respectively.

voices.title: Milnor exposition standard
voices.description: Eight hallmarks of mathematical exposition, scored 0-2 each with sixteen the only passing total, derived from John Milnor's "Link Groups" (Annals of Mathematics 59(2), 1954, pp. 177-195). Not a house standard named after him any more: every rule now cites a page of the paper, and three of them exist because the paper CONTRADICTS what this platform's own house voice asserts. 8899 words, 496 sentences, measured 2026-09-19.

sources.title: Link Groups (John Milnor, Annals of Mathematics, Second Series, 59(2), March 1954, pp. 177-195)

rules.title: H1 — Economy: the opening is a Summary, not an Introduction
rules.description: Milnor's §1 is titled "Summary" and runs about 200 words. In them: what link homotopy is, the purpose of the paper, the tool, what the tool is, and all four results. No preamble, no literature survey, no statement of what the reader will find in section 3. 0 if a paragraph could be deleted with no loss. 1 if sentences restate their neighbours, or a closing line summarises what was just said. 2 when nothing can be removed without losing content.
rules.quote: 1. Summary — By a link homotopy is meant a deformation of one link onto another, during which each component of the link is allowed to cross itself, but such that no two components are allowed to intersect. The purpose of this paper is to study links under the relation of homotopy. The fundamental tool in this study will be the link group.

rules.title: H2 — Concrete before abstract, at the scale of the PAPER not the section
rules.description: Read §2 alone and it opens on pure abstraction: "Let M be an open 3-dimensional manifold which possesses a regular triangulation. Let C be a circle." A rubric applied per section would score that 0. It is a 2, because §1 has already given the concrete picture in words a reader can hold — a deformation in which each component may cross itself but no two components may meet. The informal instance precedes the formal definition by one section. So score H2 over the unit a reader actually reads through, and never on a definitions section in isolation.
rules.quote: 2. The basic theorems — Let M be an open 3-dimensional manifold which possesses a regular triangulation. Let C be a circle. By an n-link L will be meant an ordered collection (l1, …, ln) of maps li: C -> M, where the images l1(C), …, ln(C) are to be disjoint.

rules.title: H3 — Name the tool's purpose before defining the tool
rules.description: "The fundamental tool in this study will be the link group" comes before "The link group of a link is a factor group of the fundamental group of its complement". The reader is told what the object is FOR in the sentence before they are told what it IS. 0 if a construction appears with no indication of what it is for; 1 if the motivation is present but buried after it; 2 when the purpose arrives first.
rules.quote: The fundamental tool in this study will be the link group. The link group of a link is a factor group of the fundamental group of its complement, which is invariant under homotopy.

rules.title: H4 — A symbol is introduced where it is needed and then carries weight
rules.description: Milnor introduces G(L), Ai(L), [Ai] and the product E = [A1][A2]…[An] in four consecutive sentences, each at the moment it is needed and each used thereafter; and he gives the image of a link the short name |L| because it recurs constantly. Nothing is defined for symmetry. 0 for notation used once, for collisions, or for a decorated symbol where a word would do; 1 for more indices than the argument needs; 2 when every symbol earns its name. Fixing this is not local — notation is shared across a chapter, so check what else binds a symbol before renaming it.
rules.quote: Denote the image l1(C) ∪ … ∪ ln(C) of a link L by |L|. For each proper link L let G(L) denote the fundamental group of the complement M - |L|. … Denote the kernel of this homomorphism by Ai(L), and denote the commutator subgroup of Ai by [Ai]. Since the [Ai] are normal subgroups of G(L), their product E = [A1][A2] … [An] is also a normal subgroup.

rules.title: H5 — Routine verification is dispatched in a sentence, never promoted to a lemma
rules.description: "Clearly the relation of homotopy is reflexive, symmetric and transitive." One sentence, no lemma, no proof. Promoting that to a numbered lemma would have cost the reader a context switch for nothing. 0 for a forward reference to a result not yet stated; 1 for an aside the reader must park and return to; 2 when it reads once, top to bottom. Score this on the FIRST reading: a second pass already knows the argument and cannot recover the property.
rules.quote: Two links L and L' will be called homotopic if there exist homotopies hi between the maps li and the maps l'i so that the sets h1t(C), …, hnt(C) are disjoint for each value of t. Clearly the relation of homotopy is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

rules.title: H6 — State the shape of the proof, then execute it
rules.description: The most transferable pattern in the paper. Lemma 3's proof opens by saying what will be built and why that finishes the job — "A natural isomorphism … will be constructed for i = 0, 1. Since a homotopy … induces a homotopy equivalence …, this will complete the proof" — and only then constructs it. The reader knows the destination before the first step, so no step is a surprise. 0 when the argument exists only in the displays and the prose says "we compute"; 1 when the prose narrates steps without saying why they follow; 2 when a reader who skipped every display would still follow the argument.
rules.quote: The proof will be valid for any cohomology theory. Let Q0 and Q1 denote the mapping cylinders of h0 and h1. A natural isomorphism between Hr(Z, hi(Y)) and Hr(Qi, Y) will be constructed for i = 0, 1. Since a homotopy between h0 and h1 induces a homotopy equivalence between the pairs (Q0, Y) and (Q1, Y), this will complete the proof.

rules.title: H7 — Say what the method requires, in one clause
rules.description: "The proof will be valid for any cohomology theory." Seven words telling the reader the argument does not depend on a choice they might have worried about. Milnor also situates the work against the neighbouring literature in a footnote rather than a survey section — one sentence on K. Chen's factor groups, placed where a reader who wondered would look. 0 for a heavy method with no indication why; 1 for the right tool used without saying what the alternative would have cost; 2 when the reader can see why this tool and not the obvious other one.
rules.quote: The proof will be valid for any cohomology theory.

rules.title: H8 — Measured: no superlatives, one hedge, zero second person
rules.description: H8 is the hallmark that can be counted, and the counts are the standard. Over 8899 words: ZERO instances of surprisingly, remarkably, interestingly, beautiful or elegant; ONE hedge ("a (possibly redundant) list") and it qualifies a mathematical fact rather than the author's confidence; ten uses of "may", all permissive rather than epistemic; zero "you"; zero "our"; zero "the author". Milnor never tells the reader what is important. 0 when the text tells the reader what is beautiful, surprising or important; 1 when it hedges a claim it can support; 2 when it states what is true and lets the reader judge.
rules.quote: A study of this group therefore, not only gives a method for distinguishing between links which are not homotopic, but also gives a procedure for obtaining a (possibly redundant) list of all homotopy classes of links with a given number of components.

rules.title: "Clearly" is proof economy — 14 uses in the exemplar, and the checker now knows
rules.description:
The judgement half of a criterion that has been narrowed because of it. `voice-editorializing` used to fail a block for `clearly`, and failed this very paper 26 times across 11 of its 20 pages — about twenty of them proof economy, four a term of art (`naturally isomorphic`), and exactly ONE a real finding ("Unfortunately these invariants are not strong enough", p194). Bean `2t41` narrowed the checker: the exemplar now scores that one finding and no others.

The rule stays because the mechanical half cannot make the distinction that matters. `clearly` before a verification the reader can perform is correct — it routes their effort away from something routine, which is the opposite of spending it on the author's opinion. `clearly` attached to a claim the reader CANNOT check in their head is the real defect: the author asserting where they should be proving. No phrase list separates those, and the checker's exemption is deliberately a construction test rather than a word test, which approximates it without deciding it. A reviewer deciding whether a given `clearly` earns its place is doing the part no regex can.
rules.quote: Clearly the relation of homotopy is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. … The inclusion map (Z, hi(Y)) -> (Qi, Pi) is clearly a homotopy equivalence. … The 2-link illustrated in Figure 3 is clearly trivial. … The single invariant μ(12) is clearly the linking number.

rules.title: "I" for the acknowledgement, "we" for the mathematics — and nothing else
rules.description: The second rule that corrects this platform's house voice. `one-voice-style-guide.md` says "'we' for joint reasoning with the reader, never 'I'". Milnor's split is sharper than the prohibition: exactly ONE first-person singular in the whole paper — "I am indebted to R. H. Fox for assistance in the preparation of this paper", placed at the end of §1 — against twenty uses of "we", every one of them joint reasoning ("Thus we have obtained a complete set of homotopy invariants"). Zero "our", zero "the author". So the rule is not "never I": it is that a personal debt is stated personally and in one sentence, and the mathematics is done together with the reader.
rules.quote: I am indebted to R. H. Fox for assistance in the preparation of this paper.

rules.title: Median sentence 17 words; a 50-word sentence is the outlier, not the register
rules.description: Measured over the paper's 496 sentences: median 17 words, 90th percentile 29, longest 52. This is a diagnostic rather than a rule to enforce line by line — a block whose median runs to 30 is not automatically wrong, but it is not written in this voice either, and the usual cause is clauses doing the work that a full stop and a new subject would do better.
rules.quote: Every link with two components is almost trivial. The single invariant μ(12) is clearly the linking number: hence the linking number is a complete homotopy invariant for 2-links. A link with three components is almost trivial if each pair of components has linking number zero.

rules.title: No content repeated within the block — and the resolve discipline is stricter
rules.description:
Milnor does not restate: where a result is needed again he names it and points at it. The cited sentence is the sharpest instance — the assertion about meridian and parallel pairs could have been proved by reproducing the proof of Theorem 1 with the new pairs substituted in, and instead the reader is sent back through the existing proof. The paper does this throughout, invoking numbered results by number ("by Lemma 7", "It follows from Lemma 4", "hence by Theorem 5") rather than re-deriving them.

So: no content is repeated within a block. THE RESOLVE DISCIPLINE BELOW IS THIS PROJECT'S, NOT MILNOR'S, and is stated here rather than in the citation because it is about editing rather than about the paper — a repeat may be deleted ONLY where the two occurrences are semantically identical. Where the content differs you may not delete, and you never delete maths: a diagram, an equation or a derivation. Where de-duplication would lose distinct content, keep it, or split the block if that aids explication.
rules.quote: The proof is easily given: it is only necessary to check this assertion through each stage of the proof of Theorem 1.

voices.title: Technical Writer — SDO register with RFC 2119 requirement levels
voices.description: The voice for technical documentation of standards, software and knowledge assets, written as an SDO writes (W3C, IHE). Requirement levels are RFC 2119's, read from the ingested RFC rather than from memory, and constrained by RFC 8174: only UPPERCASE usage carries the defined meaning. Applies to drafting AND to review QA. Nine rules; five cite the two ingested RFCs, three cite the `technical-documentation` skill, a node of this instance's own knowledge graph, because a rule that cites a document it was not read from is the false provenance this schema exists to prevent.

sources.title: RFC 2119 — Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels (S. Bradner, Harvard University, BCP 14, March 1997)
RFC 8174 — Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words (B. Leiba, BCP 14, May 2017)

provenanceFlags.detail: declares "assertion" — a voice read from outside this project — while 3 of 9 rule(s) cite a node of this project's own graph. That part of it is a house standard. A voice may legitimately be a synthesis of both; this asks whether the declared value still describes the result, and only a person can answer it

rules.title: MUST, REQUIRED and SHALL mean an absolute requirement — nothing weaker
rules.description: Use MUST, REQUIRED or SHALL only where the requirement is absolute. They are interchangeable by the RFC's own definition, so choose one per document and keep to it rather than varying for rhythm. A MUST that a reader may reasonably decline is not a MUST; it is a SHOULD, and mislabelling it teaches readers to discount every other MUST in the document.
rules.quote: 1. MUST   This word, or the terms "REQUIRED" or "SHALL", mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification.

rules.title: MUST NOT and SHALL NOT mean an absolute prohibition
rules.description: Reserve MUST NOT and SHALL NOT for absolute prohibitions. Do not soften a prohibition into 'should not' when it is absolute, and do not inflate a discouragement into MUST NOT because it feels important.
rules.quote: 2. MUST NOT   This phrase, or the phrase "SHALL NOT", mean that the definition is an absolute prohibition of the specification.

rules.title: SHOULD and RECOMMENDED admit exceptions, and the writer owes the reader the implications
rules.description: SHOULD and RECOMMENDED mean valid reasons may exist to ignore the item — but the RFC puts a burden on the reader to understand and weigh the implications, which the writer can only discharge by stating them. A bare SHOULD with no account of what departing from it costs is an instruction the reader cannot act on.
rules.quote: 3. SHOULD   This word, or the adjective "RECOMMENDED", mean that there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course.

rules.title: Imperatives are used sparingly, and only where interoperation or harm requires them
rules.description: The RFC constrains its own key words: they are for what is actually required for interoperation, or to limit behaviour that can cause harm. They are NOT for imposing a preferred method where the method is not required. A document in which every paragraph carries a MUST has not been made rigorous; it has made its genuine requirements unfindable.
rules.quote: Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly.  In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm (e.g., limiting retransmisssions)  For example, they must not be used to try to impose a particular method on implementors where the method is not required for interoperability.

rules.title: Only UPPERCASE key words carry the requirement meaning
rules.description: RFC 8174 updates RFC 2119: only all-capitals usage has the defined special meaning. So 'the parser must handle this' is ordinary prose and 'the parser MUST handle this' is a conformance requirement, and the difference is visible rather than inferred. A reviewer MUST read lowercase 'must' as narration, and a writer who meant a requirement MUST capitalise it.
rules.quote: This document updates RFC 2119 by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

rules.title: State what not following a requirement costs
rules.description: RFC 2119 asks authors to elaborate the implications of not following a requirement, on the grounds that most implementors lack the experience and discussion that produced the specification. Generalised here beyond security: a requirement whose consequence is unstated is one a reader cannot weigh, and is the single most common reason a correct instruction is ignored.
rules.quote: Document authors should take the time to elaborate the security implications of not following recommendations or requirements as most implementors will not have had the benefit of the experience and discussion that produced the specification.

rules.title: Glossary Terms are Capitalized throughout
rules.description: A Term defined in the Glossary is Capitalized every time it is used, so a reader can tell a defined Term from the same word used loosely. Before introducing a term, ask whether it is defined; if not, whether it is defined later, whether it belongs in the Glossary, and whether it is used in several places or only here. A term used once and nowhere else does not earn a Glossary entry.
rules.quote: Glossary Terms are Capitalized on every use, so a reader can tell a defined Term from the same word used loosely.

rules.title: After the first draft: repetition, order, defined terms
rules.description: Three questions the writer runs against their own draft before review. Have I repeated anything? If so, consolidate — the same fact in two places is free to drift, and the copy a reader finds first is the one with no test. Does the content flow in logical order? If not, apply the detangler rather than reordering by taste. Is each Term defined? This is a drafting rule, not a reviewer's courtesy: it is cheapest to fix while the draft is still the author's.
rules.quote: Have I repeated anything? If so, consolidate. The same fact in two places is free to drift, and the copy a reader finds first is usually the one with no test behind it.

rules.title: Link the schema source and its UML when the prose names a schema
rules.description: Naming a schema without linking it makes the reader guess which file is meant, and the guess fails precisely when the schema has moved. Link the source, and the UML documentation where one exists. This is the resolve-do-not-compose rule applied to prose: a written-out path is a composition nothing checks, a link is a reference a checker can falsify.
rules.quote: When the prose names a schema, link to the schema source and to its UML documentation where one exists. A schema named but not linked forces the reader to guess which file, and the guess is wrong exactly when the schema has moved.

voices.title: WHO digital health terminology
voices.description: The controlled vocabulary WHO uses to describe digital health implementations: what a digital health intervention is against the software that delivers it, what separates a bottleneck from a health system challenge, and how the two editions of the classification name themselves — including the first edition's title, which WHO says was wrong. Derived rule by rule from the ingested publications; every rule cites the section it was read from.

sources.title: Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health, second edition
Classification of Digital Health Interventions v1.0
Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG): integrating digital interventions into health programmes

rules.title: The current abbreviation is CDISAH
rules.description: The second edition is the *Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health*, and the abbreviation it introduces itself with is **CDISAH**, with the leading C. Use CDISAH for the current classification and CDHI only when referring specifically to the 2018 first edition. Two things make this counterintuitive. CDHI is the abbreviation in wide circulation and in most secondary literature, so the familiar term is the wrong one. And the publication is not internally consistent: page 9 writes the bare form 'DISAH' once, while page 7 and the classification's own short link (bit.ly/CDISAH) use CDISAH. WHO's implementation authority settles it — `WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base` uses CDISAH throughout its FHIR artefacts (`input/fsh/codesystems/CDHIv2.fsh`, `input/fsh/conceptmaps/CDHIv1toCDHIv2.fsh`) and the bare form appears in no FSH or prose there. That divergence inside one publication is the plainest argument for this voice existing at all.
rules.quote: The updated Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health (CDISAH) is a set of categorizations that links how digital health interventions

rules.title: A digital health intervention is a capability, not a system
rules.description: A digital health intervention is a discrete technology FUNCTIONALITY — a capability — such as decision support, targeted client communications or stock notification. The software that delivers it is a digital health application, or in the classification's terms a Service or Application type, such as an LMIS or an EMR. The two are different levels and an application typically delivers several interventions. Naming a product where an intervention belongs collapses the distinction the whole classification rests on.
rules.quote: DIGITAL HEALTH INTERVENTION: A discrete technology functionality – or capability – designed to achieve a specific objective addressing a health system challenge. Examples of digital health interventions include decision support, targeted client communications, and stock notifications

rules.title: A bottleneck is specific; a health system challenge is general
rules.description: A bottleneck is a gap or problem in the workflow of ONE health programme area, persona or process — DIIG's own example is health workers having difficulty tracking when pregnant women are due for an antenatal care visit. A health system challenge is the general form of that problem across any programme area, such as loss to follow-up. DIIG Chapter 3 maps the first onto the second, so treating them as synonyms destroys the step. The classification groups health system challenges into nine overarching categories: information, availability, quality, acceptability, utilization, efficiency, cost, accountability and equity.
rules.quote: BOTTLENECKS: Specific gaps or problems in the workflow of delivering health services specific to a health programme area, persona or process (for example, “health workers have difficulty keeping track of when pregnant women are due for an antenatal care visit”), in contrast to a health system challenge, which is a general representation of the problem across any health programme area (for example, “loss to follow-up”).

rules.title: 'Persons' is the classification's term, not 'patients'
rules.description: The classification groups interventions by targeted primary user, and the group covering members of the public is *Persons* — potential or current users of health services, including prevention and wellness. The classification explicitly notes that 'patients', 'clients' and 'health service users' have been used for this group; they are prior terms, not the classification's. Use Persons when writing against the classification's groupings. Outside that context an ordinary word is fine; this rule is about the taxonomy, not about banning 'patient' from English.
rules.quote: Interventions for Persons: Persons are members of the public who are potential or current users of health services, including health prevention and wellness activities. Other terms that have been used to describe individuals in this group include ‘patients’, ‘clients’ and ‘health service users’.

rules.title: An intervention is stated against a challenge and an outcome
rules.description: The classification's stated purpose is to let a planner express what they expect to achieve, and its worked form is a triple: one implements a digital health intervention IN ORDER TO address a health system challenge, TO ACHIEVE an outcome. Prose that names an intervention with no challenge and no outcome has described a capability and asserted nothing about why it was chosen — which is the gap DIIG Chapter 4 exists to close.
rules.quote: one may implement a digital health intervention, such as “targeted communication to persons”, in order to address a health system challenge, such as “lack of service utilisation,” to achieve an overarching eHealth outcome of “improving individuals’ access to knowledge resources and support for better management of their health”

rules.title: 'Digital health' is the current term; 'eHealth' is its predecessor
rules.description: DIIG defines digital health as the systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science and data to support informed decision-making. Where its glossary carries the older term it marks it as an alternative — a digital health outcome 'may also be known as an eHealth outcome', a digital health strategy as an eHealth strategy. Prefer digital health; keep eHealth when quoting a source that uses it, or when naming a national strategy by its actual title.
rules.quote: DIGITAL HEALTH OUTCOME: The desired change in the health system or services by using digital health interventions. May also be known as an eHealth outcome

rules.title: Implementation, investment and costed plan are three things
rules.description: A digital health IMPLEMENTATION is the development and deployment of applications or platforms with its governance framework, operational plan and human resources. A digital health INVESTMENT is the financial and human resources directed towards implementations. A COSTED IMPLEMENTATION PLAN is the document describing challenges with a financially justified deployment and monitoring plan, and it is what DIIG exists to produce. Using them interchangeably makes it impossible to say whether a sentence is about work, money or a document.
rules.quote: accompanied by a governance framework, operational plan, human resources and related activities for its successful execution

rules.title: The first edition's title was incorrect and is being reissued
rules.description: WHO states that the first edition was published under the wrong title. It went out as *Classification of digital health interventions v1.0* under reference WHO/RHR/18.06 — the document ingested here as `who-rhr-1806-eng` — and is being reissued under the correct title, *Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health*. So the two editions do not differ only by content: the earlier NAME is disowned by the publisher. When citing the first edition, cite it by its reference number and say which title you are using, because a reader who looks it up may find either. Do not silently modernise a v1 citation to the new title, and do not treat the v1 title as merely superseded — WHO calls it incorrect.
rules.quote: The first edition of this publication was published under the following title “Classification of digital health interventions v1.0: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health” with a WHO reference number - WHO/RHR/18.06. The first edition is being reissued under the correct title

voices.title: WHO Digital Transformation Handbook
voices.description: The register of WHO's Digital Transformation Handbooks (DTHs) — the guidance publications that take one area of a health system from paper to digital within the DIIG process: the order of digitization, digitalization and digital transformation, what a registry is against a register, what master data excludes, and how the draft DPI-H Reference Architecture names its own layers. Derived rule by rule from the three DTHs and the draft Reference Architecture ingested in smart-base/library; every rule cites the section it was read from, and a rule resting on the DRAFT says so.

sources.title: Digital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems
Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture
Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue
Reference Architecture and Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for the Health Sector — A Digital Transformation Handbook for Digital Public Infrastructure for Health (DPI-H), DRAFT V1.0

rules.title: Digitization, digitalization and digital transformation are three different scopes
rules.description: The handbooks define the three terms narrowly. Digitization is converting paper records into digital format; digitalization is automating and simplifying processes WITHIN individual health programmes; digital transformation is systems-level change across all programme areas. Whether they are also an ORDERED sequence is where the sources differ, and both readings are on record as alternatives (smart-base/findings/dth-terms.md; owner, 2026-10-03, #1984): the supply chain handbook adds that digitization is the initial step and digitalization the second, and the product catalogue handbook repeats it as steps 'towards' digital transformation, while the primary health care handbook defines the same terms without any order. So write the scope a term names, and do not assert the order as the handbooks' common position. In ordinary usage 'digitalization' is a loose synonym for going digital at any scale, and the draft DPI-H Reference Architecture itself quotes the World Bank calling DPI 'an approach to digitalization' — a broad, cross-sector sense the earlier handbooks would call digital transformation. The draft also writes 'digitalisation' and 'digitisation' alongside 'digitalization'; the published handbooks use -ization throughout. Because the draft may change, prefer the published handbooks' sense and spelling.
rules.quote: In the health context, the process of digitally automating and simplifying processes to streamline individual health programmes and reduce manual efforts for greater efficiency. Digitalization is the second step in digital transformation

rules.title: A register is a list of service users; a registry is a governed master system
rules.description: The primary health care handbook defines the two words separately and they are not variants. A register is a list of health service users compiled to track care, aggregate activity or find people needing an intervention — a paper ANC register is a register. A registry is a governed, authoritative, centralized information system holding the unique attributes and identifiers of facilities, health service users, products and/or the health workforce against a canonical minimum data set; the supply chain and product catalogue handbooks and the draft Reference Architecture carry the same registry definition. Note that the draft groups the terminology service, the logical information model repository and the lifelong health record under 'metadata registries and foundational components'; that heading does not make them registries in this sense.
rules.quote: In the context of health care, a list of health service users compiled for the purposes of tracking care, aggregating activities or health outcomes, or identifying health service users who need specific interventions.

rules.title: DPI-H is health-specific infrastructure built on foundational DPI, not DPI itself
rules.description: Rests on the DRAFT Reference Architecture (V1.0, for public comment), which may change. DPI-H names digital resources built as a shared means for multiple HEALTH agency functions; it leverages and extends foundational DPI (identity, payments, data exchange — abbreviated DPI-F) and does not replicate it. The draft is explicit that DPI-H is not a collection of programme-specific tools or point-of-service applications. Write DPI-H with the hyphen. The draft is itself inconsistent on the expansion — its acronym list and definition give 'Health Digital Public Infrastructure', its cover 'Digital Public Infrastructure for Health', and one glossary entry writes 'HDPI' — so the abbreviation, not any one expansion, is the stable form.
rules.quote: Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions.

rules.title: A PCPOSS is a category spanning several application types, not one product
rules.description: The primary health care handbook's person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) is an umbrella: community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical or health record systems and personal health records are all PCPOSS. It is spelled 'person-centred' and, in that handbook, 'point of service' without hyphens (POS is point of service, never point of sale). Do not equate a PCPOSS with an EMR. The DRAFT Reference Architecture uses a different label, 'point-of-service applications' (glossary entry marked [Under review]), and places them outside DPI-H.
rules.quote: PCPOSS encompass various services and application types, including community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical (or health) record systems and personal health records

rules.title: Product master data excludes batch numbers, serial numbers and manufacturing dates
rules.description: In the product catalogue handbook, product master data is the information that stays the same for every instance of a product: description, dosage, strength, manufacturer details, shelf life. Batch or lot numbers, manufacturing dates and serial numbers vary per instance and are transactional data. They are the identifiers a traceability discussion reaches for first, which is why they get mislabelled as master data.
rules.quote: In contrast, transactional data—such as batch numbers, manufacturing dates, and serial numbers—varies with each specific instance of the product.

rules.title: 'Generic product' means manufacturer-independent information, not a generic medicine
rules.description: The product catalogue handbook gives 'generic product', 'product' and 'product information' a handbook-specific meaning: the general identifying details of a health product, without any manufacturer-specific information. In pharmaceutical usage a 'generic' is an off-patent medicine from a non-originator manufacturer — a different idea. In catalogue prose, 'generic product' is the level above the trade item, not a market category.
rules.quote: In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information.

rules.title: A health supply chain information system can be paper-based
rules.description: The supply chain handbook defines a health supply chain information system (HSCIS) as a paper-based OR software tool, and defines an order management system the same way. 'Information system' therefore does not imply software, and an inventory of current HSCISs includes the paper forms. The handbook notes that the software tools are commonly called electronic logistics management information systems (eLMIS); eLMIS is the narrower term.
rules.quote: A paper-based or software tool that supports the management and/or operations of the health supply chain.

rules.title: 'National product catalogue' in prose; 'catalog' survives in tool names and the 2024 handbook
rules.description: The product catalogue handbook's title and body use 'catalogue' together with -ize spellings such as 'standardized' (the WHO pairing). Its own abbreviation list nevertheless expands NPC as 'National product catalog', and the earlier supply chain handbook writes 'National Product Catalog', capitalized, in its abbreviations and prose. The Product Catalog Management Tool (PCMT) is a proper name and keeps its spelling. In running prose write 'national product catalogue (NPC)', lower case, as the 2025 handbook does.
rules.quote: This handbook complements the DIIG by providing a structured approach to implementing a national product catalogue (NPC) for standardized product master data management.

rules.title: Integration is bespoke; interoperability is standards-based
rules.description: Rests on the DRAFT Reference Architecture, whose glossary marks this entry [Under review]. The draft separates integration — a bespoke connection from one application component to another — from interoperability, which it defines as a standards-based capability of heterogeneous systems. The published handbooks define interoperability through shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, and do not define integration, so the contrast is the draft's. 'Integrated with' is not a synonym for 'interoperable with' in this register.
rules.quote: Bespoke capability of connecting one application component to another [Under review]

voices.title: WHO editorial style
voices.description: The house editorial style of the World Health Organization: spelling, capitalization, eponym form, reference layout and non-discriminatory language, as set out in the WHO Editorial Style Manual. Derived rule by rule from the ingested manual; every rule cites the page it was read from.

sources.title: WHO Editorial Style Manual

rules.title: -ize, not -ise
rules.description: Where a word may be spelled with -ize or -ise, use -ize: organize, not organise; organization, not organisation. The manual's stated ground is the Greek root and the first spelling in The concise Oxford dictionary. The exception is a word where -ise is not a suffix but part of the root — surprise, comprise, improvise — which keep -ise. This rule is the reason the voice had to be derived rather than assumed: it is commonly believed that WHO house style is -ise, and PR #210 asserted exactly that.
rules.quote: Where there is a choice between using the suffix -ize or -ise (e.g. organize or organise), -ize, derived from the Greek "-izo", is preferred, consistent with the first spelling of such words given in The concise Oxford dictionary. For some words, such as surprise, comprise or improvise, where -ise is not a suffix but part of the root of the word, there is no choice.

rules.title: Crohn disease, not Crohn's disease
rules.description: An eponymous name takes no Saxon genitive: Crohn disease, Down syndrome. The manual goes further and asks that eponyms be avoided altogether where a descriptive name exists, on the ground that an eponym carries no information about the disease and may name something different in another country — so a finding here is worth reading as two questions, not one.
rules.quote: Eponymous names give no information about the nature of the disease and different names may be used in different countries. They should be avoided whenever possible. The Saxon genitive ('s) is not necessary when using an eponymous name; e.g. Crohn disease, not Crohn's disease, and Down syndrome, not Down's syndrome.

rules.title: Member State, the Organization — and headquarters, primary health care
rules.description: The manual gives two explicit lists rather than a principle, and the two halves are easy to get backwards. Capitalised: Member State, Associate Member, the Organization (meaning WHO), the Constitution, Region in a specific reference, Regional Committee, Regional Director, World Health Assembly, General Programme of Work, Global Strategy for Health for All. Lower case: headquarters, primary health care, health for all, session, resolution, decision, strategy, specialized agency, representatives, committee and commission unless specifically identified, region used generically, and names of seasons. Note the pair the manual calls out itself: member (of a committee) but Member (State).
rules.quote: The following words and expressions used frequently within WHO normally require capitalization: Associate Member; Constitution (of WHO); (Eighth) General Programme of Work; Forty-… World Health Assembly; … Member (country); Member State; … the Organization (WHO); Region [of WHO] … / The following words and expressions do not normally require capitalization: commission, committee (unless specifically identified); … health for all; headquarters (WHO); member (of the committee, etc.), but Member (State); … primary health care; … specialized agency

rules.title: Capitals break the eye; use them for names, not for importance
rules.description: Proper names, titles and institutions take capitals. Descriptive appellations — administrative posts and the like — do not, unless lower case would read oddly. A trade name takes an initial capital (Pyrex, Vaseline, with the generic preferred where one exists); a Linnaean genus takes one (Staphylococcus aureus, Trypanosoma) while the anglicised common form does not (trypanosome, schistosome). Article, book and journal titles in references are NOT capitalised except where they contain an organization's name.
rules.quote: Too many capital letters break the flow of the eye across a sentence and down a column of type. However, proper names, titles and institutions require capitals. Descriptive appellations, such as administrative posts, do not, unless the result would appear odd or confusing. … Generic terms in the Linnaean classification also take an initial capital letter, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus, Trypanosoma, Schistosoma, but trypanosome, schistosome, etc. Article, book and journal titles in references need not be capitalized, e.g. Social science and medicine, except when they contain the name of an association or organization

rules.title: All authors up to three; et al. from four
rules.description: List every author when there are three or fewer. From four, give the first author only and add et al. Author names are surname followed by initials with no periods and no comma between them — Cairns RB, DuPont B, Crompton DWT et al.
rules.quote: 1. List all authors when three or fewer; when four or more, give only first author's name and add et al.

rules.title: Write journal names out in full
rules.description: No abbreviated journal titles. The manual's reason is worth keeping with the rule, because it decides the borderline cases: it is for readers whose first language is not English, who cannot expand an unfamiliar abbreviation. So 'Bulletin of the World Health Organization', never 'Bull World Health Organ'.
rules.quote: 2. Write out journal names in full. This is particularly helpful to readers whose mother tongue is not English.

rules.title: Rewrite, do not decorate: the non-discriminatory pairs
rules.description: The manual's own table, which is prescriptive about the TECHNIQUE and not only the vocabulary. Its four general rules are: delete redundant possessive pronouns; rephrase; use the first person plural; and use neutral or equivalent job titles. Its worked substitutions include foreman/workman/office girl/policeman becoming supervisor/worker/secretary or receptionist or office assistant/police officer; 'Man, mankind' and 'the average man' rephrased; 'show the mother how to cook' becoming 'show members of the family', on the stated ground that women are not assumed to do the household chores; 'ask mothers to bring their children' becoming 'ask parents', because men have responsibility for children too; and 'Mrs John Smith' becoming 'Jane Smith'.
rules.quote: Common discriminatory phrases / Useful solutions / Useful general rules … Delete redundant possessive pronouns … Use the first person plural … Foreman, workman, office girl, policeman → Supervisor, worker, secretary, receptionist, office assistant, police officer → Use neutral or equivalent job titles … Show the mother how to cook nutritious meals → Show members of the family how to cook nutritious meals → Do not assume that women always do the household chores … Ask mothers to bring their children to the clinic each month → Ask parents to bring their children to the clinic each month → Remember that men have responsibility for children too

rules.title: The rewrite is not more cumbersome — that is the manual's own claim
rules.description: The manual anticipates the objection that non-discriminatory phrasing is clumsy and answers it with worked pairs of equal length, moving to the plural rather than to 'he or she': 'He may see himself as the pivot of all that happens … may comment on the patient or address him' becomes 'Patients may see themselves as the pivot of all that happens … may comment on or address patients'. So a reviewer should reject 'he or she' and 's/he' patches and ask for the plural or a rephrase. It also asks that research involving both sexes report both, and that gross figures in statistical reports be broken down by sex unless no significant difference has already been established.
rules.quote: With care, the results of rewriting text to eliminate discriminatory language will be no less concise than the original — but will be unambiguous and will avoid causing offence. … In reporting research of any kind that involves both men and women and/or children of both sexes, both males and females should be mentioned in the results. In statistical reports, gross figures should be broken down by sex unless it has previously been established that there is no significant difference between the sexes.

rules.title: Country names are checked, not remembered
rules.description: The manual is explicit that country names and their spellings change 'at an alarming rate' and names the office that holds the current list, with full, short and adjectival forms. The rule for an author or an agent is therefore procedural: do not spell a Member State's name from memory or from an older document in the same corpus. This is judgement-only by construction — no pattern can know which name was current when a passage was written.
rules.quote: Webster's new geographical dictionary … can be used as a guide to the spelling of common geographical entities. However, country names and their spelling, in particular, can change at an alarming rate. The Computer-Assisted Translation and Terminology subunit (CTT), which coordinates with the Office of the Legal Counsel (LEG), can provide up-to-date information on the names of United Nations and WHO Member States, including their full, short and adjectival/attributive forms.

rules.title: Follow The concise Oxford dictionary's first spelling — and Annex 1 where WHO differs
rules.description: The general spelling rule the manual's Annex 1 opens with: take the spelling The concise Oxford dictionary gives first, or the one a variant entry refers you to. Annex 1 then lists WHO's own exceptions and the words that most often cause doubt; the rules who-ed-spelling-annex-p088 to p102 carry that list, one rule per printed page, each quoting its page. Where a word is not listed, this rule decides.
rules.quote: The general rule in WHO is to follow the spelling given in the latest edition of The concise Oxford dictionary; where it gives alternative spellings or forms, use the one given first (e.g. fulfil, fulfill) or the one to which you are referred from an entry giving a variant spelling (e.g. "tire, US var. of tyre": use "tyre").
