voices.title: WHO guideline development
voices.description: How a WHO recommendation is worded and what must travel with it: strength, certainty, justification, remarks and a link to the evidence. Derived from the WHO handbook for guideline development, 2nd edition. This voice governs the language of normative statements, not the process that produces them — the process is the handbook's subject and belongs in a workflow, not a style rule.

sources.title: WHO handbook for guideline development, 2nd ed.

rules.title: "should" is strong; "suggest" or "consider" is conditional
rules.description: GRADE's wording convention, adopted by the handbook: a strong recommendation uses "should" or "strongly recommend"; a conditional one uses "suggest" or "consider". The two vocabularies must not be mixed, because the verb is how a reader learns the strength — a conditional recommendation phrased with "should" reads as strong and will be implemented as one.
rules.quote: GRADE recommends using terms or phrases such as "should" or "strongly recommend" for strong recommendations, and "suggest" or "consider" for conditional ones.

rules.title: Never "not recommended" — say "we recommend against X"
rules.description: The handbook singles this phrase out as ambiguous, and names both readings: it can mean that no recommendation either way was made, or that the intervention should not be implemented. Where the second is meant, the required wording is "we recommend against intervention X…". This is the one rule in the voice whose severity is about reader safety rather than register: the two readings lead to opposite clinical actions.
rules.quote: The use of confusing or ambiguous phrases should be avoided. For example, the phrase "not recommended" could be interpreted to mean either that no recommendation for or against the intervention has been made, or that the intervention should not be implemented. In the latter instance, "we recommend against intervention X…" is the preferred wording.

rules.title: Recommendations are written in the active voice, and worded consistently
rules.description: The handbook asks for the active voice and for consistency across every recommendation in one guideline. Consistency is the harder half and the one a per-block check cannot see: it is a property of the set, so a reviewer must read the recommendations together rather than one at a time.
rules.quote: The language of each recommendation is critically important. Wherever possible, it should be consistent across all recommendations in a guideline, which should be written in the active voice.

rules.title: Keep outcomes out of the recommendation itself
rules.description: Naming an outcome in the recommendation implies that outcome was the only one considered. The handbook asks that outcomes generally stay out of the statement — they belong in the evidence summary and the remarks. A recommendation that reads "…to reduce mortality" is the shape to question.
rules.quote: Outcomes should generally not be mentioned in the recommendation to avoid the impression that only single outcomes are relevant or were considered.

rules.title: Clear, actionable, and in PICO shape
rules.description: A recommendation reflects the PICO format — population, intervention, comparator, outcome — and is actionable: a reader must be able to tell who it applies to and what to do. Combined with the rule above, the resolution is that P, I and C appear in the statement while O informs it without being named.
rules.quote: Recommendations need to be clear and actionable, reflect the PICO format and contain an indication of their strength and of the quality of the evidence on which they are based.

rules.title: State the certainty as high, moderate, low or very low
rules.description: Four levels, named exactly. A recommendation with no stated certainty is incomplete, and so is one that grades the evidence on some other scale — "strong evidence" is not a GRADE level and conflates certainty with strength, which the handbook keeps apart throughout.
rules.quote: The quality of the underlying body of evidence (high, moderate, low or very low) should be specified.

rules.title: Every recommendation carries its justification, its remarks and a link to the evidence
rules.description: Four things travel with the statement: why it is strong or conditional, why it is for or against, remarks giving the conditions and context in which it applies and what to bear in mind when implementing it, and a link to the evidence — a systematic review, the GRADE evidence profiles and the evidence-to-decision tables. A block carrying the recommendation and none of these is not yet a recommendation; in a folio this is what `uses[]` and the evidence sidecar are for.
rules.quote: A recommendation should include a justification as to why it is strong or conditional and why it is for or against a given intervention. It should also contain a set of remarks explaining the conditions and context in which the recommendation applies and the points to bear in mind regarding implementation. … Each recommendation should be linked to a summary of the evidence (e.g. a published systematic review or the systematic review in an online annex), the GRADE evidence profiles and the evidence-to-decision tables.

rules.title: A conditional recommendation names the conditions
rules.description: The handbook's account of why a recommendation is conditional — the GDG being less certain about the balance of benefits against harms — carries a drafting consequence: a conditional recommendation generally includes a description of the conditions under which the end-user should or should not implement it. So "we suggest X" with no conditions attached has the form of a conditional recommendation and not the content.
rules.quote: Recommendations that are conditional or weak are made when a GDG is less certain about the balance between the benefits and harms or disadvantages of implementing a recommendation. Conditional recommendations generally include a description of the conditions under which the end-user should or should not implement the recommendation.

voices.title: WHO publication design (Western Pacific Region)
voices.description: The visual conventions around the prose rather than the prose itself: logo use, palette, typography, pagination and figure accessibility, as set out in the WHO Western Pacific Region publication and information products style guide. This is the one voice whose rules mostly do not touch a block's text, which is why it is a separate voice rather than more rules on who-editorial — a folio can want WHO's editorial register without WPRO's brand.

sources.title: Publication and Information Products Style Guide

rules.title: Never red with green, never blue with yellow
rules.description: The guide's one hard accessibility rule for figures, and the one that matters most for a generated chart: do not combine red and green, and do not combine blue and yellow. Both pairs are the classic confusion axes. It points onward to "Accessible Publishing at WHO" for the rest. Note this agrees with this repo's own `dataviz` skill and `docs/accessibility.md`, so a folio activating this voice is not taking on a conflicting rule.
rules.quote: • Recommended font size 10pts • Avoid combining red and green. Avoid combining blue and yellow. For further information please check "Accessible Publishing at WHO"

rules.title: 10pt in graphs, figures and tables
rules.description: The recommended font size inside a figure or a table is 10pt. Stated on both the figure page and the table page, so it is the guide's setting for data presentation generally rather than a one-off.
rules.quote: Graphs and figures sample • Recommended font size 10pts … Table sample • Recommended font size 10pts

rules.title: Roman numerals for the front matter, Arabic for the body
rules.description: Preliminary pages take lower-case Roman numerals and the body takes Arabic. The guide also fixes the order of the front matter: title page; copyright, disclaimer and cataloguing behind the title page; table of contents listing chapters, figures and tables; foreword or preface; acknowledgements; list of contributors; list of abbreviations; executive summary. Then the body: chapters, references or bibliography, annexes.
rules.quote: PAGINATION Preliminary pages have lower-case Roman page numbers • Title page • Copyright + disclaimer + cataloging (behind title page) • Table of contents (list of chapters, figures and tables) • Foreword or Preface • Acknowledgments • List of contributors • List of abbreviations • Executive summary Main pages have Arabic page numbers • Chapters • References or bibliography • Annexes

rules.title: The logo is placed, never redrawn
rules.description: Do not alter, rotate or modify the logo, never recreate it, and do not obstruct it. Three versions exist — blue, black, and white on a dark background — and the logo may only appear on materials WPRO has endorsed. That last clause is a permission, not a style preference: a folio that is not a WPRO product must not carry it at all.
rules.quote: The logo for the World Health Organization Regional Office for the Western Pacific (WPRO) should only be used on materials endorsed by WPRO. It should be presented as per guidelines here. This is essential to maintain a consistent presentation of our identity. Do not alter, rotate or modify the logo. It should never be recreated. Do not obstruct the logo. Three versions: The three versions of the WPRO logo are Blue, Black and White on a dark background

rules.title: 1 cm of clear space, 3 cm minimum size
rules.description: Leave an exclusion zone of at least 1 cm on every side of the logo, equal on all sides, and never reproduce it below 3 cm — the guide's stated floor for legibility in print and on screen. Where it sits beside another logo the clear space is no less than a quarter of the logo's width.
rules.quote: Leave "exclusion zones" around the logos (at least 1cm width distance) around the logos to ensure they maintain visual impact. Also the minimum logo size is 3cm (the smallest size at which the logo is still legible in print and on screen) For other sizes, no less than 1/4 width of logo. … Clear space should be equal on all sides.

rules.title: The regional blue is C95 M25 Y0 K0 / R0 G147 B213
rules.description: The primary logo blue, given in both CMYK and RGB. A folio reproducing the brand takes the values from the guide rather than sampling them from an image — a sampled colour is a colour that drifted.

rules.title: One of four typefaces, for brand recognition rather than taste
rules.description: News Gothic MT, DIN OT, PT Sans or Calibri, each with its stated weights; Times New Roman appears with a sample as well. The guide's reason is family resemblance across WHO products, which is why it is a rule rather than a suggestion, and why substituting a similar-looking font defeats it. Body samples are set at 10pt with leading of 12–13pt.
rules.quote: Consistent fonts across our communications help brand recognition. This helps people recognize WHO publications and communications as part of the same family and gives our products a professional look and feel. News Gothic MT (bold, regular, italic) • DIN OT (bold, medium, regular, italic, condense, condense medium, light, light italic) PT Sans (bold, regular, italic, narrow, narrow regular) • Calibri (bold, regular, italic, light italic, light)

rules.title: Prefer WHO images, and credit them
rules.description: Photographs should come from the Regional Office or the WHO photo library where possible, and carry credits. A folio's figure with no credit line is the finding here — the same provenance discipline the rest of this platform applies to a measurement or a quotation.
rules.quote: Photos and credits It is best to use WHO images from the Regional Office or WHO photo library
